title: Emotional and Social Disorders
summary: Four emotional and social disorders of childhood: reactive attachment disorder, separation anxiety disorder, phobias including school phobia, and childhood depression.

lesson.title: When early care fails
lesson.hook: Two toddlers from the same understaffed orphanage meet a visitor. One freezes, watching silently, refusing to be held. The other runs to the stranger and climbs into their lap. Both behaviours, opposite as they look, can come from the same early neglect.

steps.title: Reactive attachment disorder
steps.detail: Disturbed ability to relate to others after early neglect or abuse.

steps.title: Separation anxiety disorder
steps.detail: Excessive fear of being apart from parents or caregivers.

steps.title: Phobias
steps.detail: Extreme fears out of proportion to real danger, such as school phobia.

steps.title: Childhood depression
steps.detail: Persistent sadness, irritability and withdrawal in children.

slides.heading: What it is
slides.body:
**Reactive attachment disorder (RAD)** is a marked disturbance in a child's ability to **relate to other people**, beginning **before age five**. Affected children fail to show the **social attachments** normal for their age.

Attachment theory (Bowlby) holds that infants need a consistent, responsive caregiver to form secure bonds. When that care is missing, the capacity to bond can be damaged.

left.title: Inhibited
points: Fails to start or respond to social contact
Watchful, constantly observing others
Resists physical contact and comfort

right.title: Disinhibited
points: Indiscriminate with people
Little fear of unfamiliar adults; approaches them
Treats strangers like family, seeks lots of contact

slides.question: A four-year-old warmly hugs and follows any stranger as readily as her own carers. This fits which subtype of RAD?
slides.why: Indiscriminate approach to strangers, treating them like familiar people, marks the disinhibited subtype.

slides.heading: Neglect is part of the diagnosis
slides.body:
Unusually, the diagnosis requires a **history**, not just symptoms. The child must have experienced **serious neglect or outright abuse** before the symptoms began. **Inadequate care** is assumed to cause the syndrome.

In the later DSM-5, the disinhibited pattern became a separate diagnosis, **disinhibited social engagement disorder**.

slides.question: Which subtype of reactive attachment disorder involves resisting comfort and constantly watching others?
slides.why: The inhibited subtype withdraws and resists contact; the disinhibited subtype is indiscriminately friendly.

slides.heading: Lessons from orphanages
slides.story: After 1989, thousands of children were found in severely understaffed Romanian orphanages with almost no individual care. Many, once adopted, struggled to form attachments or were overly friendly with strangers. Those adopted earlier generally did better than those adopted later, a pattern researchers followed for years.
slides.takeaway: Severe early deprivation can disrupt attachment; earlier placement in a caring family improves outcomes.

slides.heading: Limited research, debated treatments
slides.body:
Because RAD was a relatively **new** diagnostic category in DSM-IV, there has been **little research** on how common it is, its specific causes, or which treatments work.

Some practitioners promote particular therapies; others **doubt** they are appropriate. Most experts agree the priority is a **stable, caring, responsive caregiver**.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'identify four emotional and social disorders' and 'discuss reactive attachment disorder'. Key points: onset before five, two subtypes, required history of neglect or abuse, little research. Trap: thinking RAD can be diagnosed from symptoms alone; the neglect history is part of the criteria.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following is a requirement for diagnosing reactive attachment disorder? (a) onset after age ten (b) a history of serious neglect or abuse before symptoms (c) a fear of school (d) low serotonin
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Add onset before age five and describe both subtypes.

points: Four disorders: RAD, separation anxiety disorder, phobias, childhood depression.
RAD: disturbed relating to others, beginning before age five.
Inhibited subtype withdraws; disinhibited subtype is indiscriminately friendly.
Diagnosis requires a history of serious neglect or abuse.
Research is limited; a stable caring home is the priority.

questions.stem: Reactive attachment disorder begins before the age of:
questions.explanation: The disturbance begins before age five.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four emotional and social disorders discussed?
questions.explanation: Dyslexia is a learning disorder, not one of the four emotional and social disorders.

questions.stem: The two subtypes of reactive attachment disorder are:
questions.explanation: RAD has inhibited and disinhibited subtypes.

questions.stem: The inhibited subtype of RAD is marked by:
options: Persistent failure to start or respond to social contact
questions.explanation: Inhibited children withdraw, watch others and resist comfort.

questions.stem: RAD is assumed to be caused mainly by:
questions.explanation: Serious neglect or abuse, meaning inadequate care, is assumed to cause it.

questions.stem: Why is relatively little known about RAD's prevalence and treatment?
options: It was a new diagnostic category in DSM-IV
questions.explanation: As a newer category, it had attracted little research.

questions.stem: A three-year-old raised in a neglectful home stiffens when hugged, watches others silently and never seeks comfort. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Withdrawal and resisting comfort after neglect fit the inhibited subtype.

questions.stem: A child adopted from an under-resourced orphanage happily goes off with any adult who smiles at him. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Lack of wariness and indiscriminate approach to strangers marks the disinhibited subtype.

questions.stem: A clinician sees a withdrawn four-year-old but finds no history of neglect or abuse. Can RAD be diagnosed?
options: No, a history of serious neglect or abuse is required
Yes, if the child is shy
questions.explanation: The criteria include a history of pathogenic care before symptoms began.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes RAD's disinhibited subtype from normal friendliness?
options: Treating strangers and familiar carers the same way, with no wariness
questions.explanation: Normal children prefer familiar carers and show some wariness of strangers.

questions.stem: In DSM-5, the disinhibited pattern of RAD became:
questions.explanation: DSM-5 separated it as disinhibited social engagement disorder.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of RAD EXCEPT:
options: It is caused mainly by high intelligence
It requires a history of neglect or abuse
questions.explanation: RAD is linked to inadequate care, not intelligence.

questions.stem: I. RAD has inhibited and disinhibited subtypes. II. Treatments for RAD are well established by extensive research. III. Inadequate care is assumed to cause RAD. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Research on RAD treatment is limited and some therapies are disputed.

questions.stem: Research on children adopted from severely deprived orphanages suggests that outcomes are generally better when children are:
questions.explanation: Earlier placement in responsive care tends to improve attachment outcomes.

questions.stem: Which model of abnormality most directly explains RAD as described in the course?
options: A model stressing early caregiving environment and relationships
questions.explanation: RAD is defined by inadequate early care, pointing to environmental and relational explanations.

lesson.title: Fears that take over
lesson.hook: Every morning, nine-year-old Ife gets a stomach ache at the school gate, then feels fine by 10am at home. Her mother wonders if she is pretending. She is not. Something real is going on.

slides.heading: Normal separation anxiety
slides.body:
**Separation anxiety**, fear and distress when apart from parents or caregivers, is a **normal** part of development. It usually begins around **8 or 9 months**, **peaks about 14 months**, then gradually fades.

Its onset matches the development of **object permanence**: the understanding that people and objects still exist when out of sight. (Your notes print this as 'object romance'.) Babies cry or become distressed when separated.

slides.heading: Separation anxiety disorder
slides.body:
When separation anxiety **continues well into childhood**, or returns later, it may be **separation anxiety disorder**. Children worry excessively that their **parents will die, fall ill**, or be lost through **kidnapping or accidents**.

They fear being alone, may **refuse school**, demand attention, insist someone stays at bedtime, and may get **headaches or nausea** when separation looms. Sometimes it continues into **adulthood**.

slides.question: Normal separation anxiety typically peaks at about:
slides.why: It begins around 8 to 9 months, peaks about 14 months, then subsides.

slides.heading: Causes and treatment
slides.body:
Causes are **unclear**, but symptoms often appear after the child **loses** someone or something loved, for example when a grandparent or a pet dies.

Treatment involves **gradual exposure** to separation (such as attending school) and teaching the child to manage **anxiety and irrational thoughts**. Therapists also work with **parents** so that **overprotection** does not accidentally feed the anxiety.

slides.heading: From fear to phobia
slides.body:
Childhood **fears are universal**, though their **content and intensity** differ by culture and change with **age**: toddlers fear strangers and noises, older children fear the dark, monsters or injury.

A fear becomes a **phobia** when it is **out of proportion** to the real danger the object presents, so extreme that the child may become **immobilised**.

left.title: School phobia
points: Often a good student who wants to attend
Intense anxiety: toilet trips, sickness, sweating
Stays home; parents know where the child is

right.title: Truancy
points: Avoids school deliberately
No anxiety about school itself
Parents often unaware the child is absent

slides.heading: Treating school phobia
slides.body:
School phobia is among the **most common and troublesome** childhood phobias. Its causes are not always separation fear; they can include **social or academic fears**, **depression**, or fear of **specific people or objects** at school.

Effective behavioural treatment uses **desensitisation**, gradual exposure to the feared situation, plus **work with parents**, who monitor the child and learn to spot any behaviour of their own that **subtly maintains** the phobia.

slides.heading: The hidden fear
slides.story: A 13-year-old, Sara, was referred for fears of planes, bees and lifts. As trust grew, her therapist found one fear beneath them all: anaesthesia. During an earlier tooth extraction under general anaesthetic, everything went dark while she could still hear rushing voices, which terrified her. She now avoided anything that might send her to hospital. Relaxation training ended her difficulties within three months.
slides.takeaway: Several phobias may share one underlying fear; finding it, and teaching relaxation, can resolve them.

slides.question: How does a child with school phobia usually differ from a truant?
options: The truant feels intense anxiety about school
The child with school phobia hates learning
The child with school phobia stays at home, and parents know where they are
slides.why: School-phobic children often want to attend but are overwhelmed by anxiety and stay home; truants' parents are often unaware.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'discuss separation anxiety and phobias in children'. Know the normal timeline (8 to 9 months, peak 14 months), object permanence, signs of the disorder, treatment, and school phobia versus truancy. Trap: treating all separation anxiety as a disorder; it is normal in infancy.
slides.sampleQuestion: A fear becomes a phobia when it is: (a) shared by many children (b) out of proportion to the real danger the object presents (c) learned from parents (d) present before age two
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). Then explain school phobia, how it differs from truancy, and treatment with desensitisation and parental involvement.

points: Separation anxiety is normal from 8 to 9 months, peaking about 14 months.
It links to object permanence.
The disorder: excessive, persistent fears for parents, school refusal, physical symptoms.
Phobia: fear out of proportion to real danger.
School phobia differs from truancy; treat with desensitisation and parent work.

questions.stem: Normal separation anxiety usually begins when a child is about:
questions.explanation: It begins around 8 or 9 months.

questions.stem: A fear becomes a phobia when it is:
options: Out of proportion to the real danger
questions.explanation: Disproportionate fear defines a phobia.

questions.stem: The ability to understand that people still exist when out of sight is called:
questions.explanation: Object permanence coincides with the onset of separation anxiety.

questions.stem: Children with separation anxiety disorder often worry that:
options: Their parents will die, fall ill or be lost
questions.explanation: Excessive fears for parents' safety are typical.

questions.stem: Symptoms of separation anxiety disorder often begin after:
options: A loss, such as a death in the family
questions.explanation: Onset often follows the death of a relative or pet.

questions.stem: An effective behavioural treatment for phobias is:
questions.explanation: Gradual exposure reduces fear.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old insists his mother sit beside him until he sleeps, refuses sleepovers and gets headaches when she travels. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Persistent excessive distress about separation in later childhood fits the disorder.

questions.stem: A bright pupil sweats and vomits every school morning but is happy at home, and her parents know she is at home. This suggests:
questions.explanation: Intense anxiety about school, with parents aware, marks school phobia.

questions.stem: A therapist helping a child with separation anxiety also works with the parents mainly to:
options: Ensure overprotection does not accidentally worsen the anxiety
questions.explanation: Overprotective responses can maintain the child's anxiety.

questions.stem: All of the following are possible causes of school phobia EXCEPT:
options: A deliberate wish to skip lessons for fun
questions.explanation: Deliberate avoidance for fun describes truancy, not phobia.

questions.stem: In the case of Sara, her fears of planes, lifts and bees were linked by an underlying fear of:
options: Anaesthesia and being taken to hospital
questions.explanation: All three could injure her and send her to hospital, where she feared anaesthesia.

questions.stem: Which statement about childhood fears is correct?
options: They are universal, though content and intensity vary by culture and age
They occur only in Western cultures
questions.explanation: Fears are universal, shaped by culture and development.

questions.stem: I. Separation anxiety is normal in infancy. II. Separation anxiety disorder can continue into adulthood. III. School phobia and truancy are the same. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. School phobia involves anxiety and parental awareness; truancy does not.

questions.stem: Why is parental involvement important in treating school phobia?
options: Parents should take the child out of school
Parents can monitor progress and identify their own behaviour that subtly maintains the phobia
questions.explanation: Parents may unknowingly reinforce avoidance, so their involvement aids recovery.

questions.stem: In Sara's case, what treatment resolved her phobias within three months?
questions.explanation: Her therapist taught relaxation techniques for anxious situations.

lesson.title: When children lose their spark
lesson.hook: For years, many experts believed young children could not really be depressed. Then researchers looked more carefully at irritable, withdrawn children complaining of constant stomach aches.

slides.heading: Children can be depressed
slides.body:
Before the **1970s**, many clinicians assumed **pre-adolescents** rarely developed depression. Research has since shown that children **can and do** develop the full syndrome.

About **2 to 4%** of children and adolescents under 17 experience **major depressive disorder**, and depression has the **highest lifetime prevalence** of the emotional disorders.

slides.heading: How it looks in children
slides.body:
**Depression** involves deep, unshakeable **sadness** and loss of interest in nearly all activities, with feelings of **despair, hopelessness and worthlessness**.

In **young children**, it often shows differently: **physical complaints** such as **stomach aches and headaches**, **irritability**, moping, **social withdrawal**, changes in **eating**, and loss of interest in school and play (APA, 2000).

slides.question: Which of these is a common sign of depression in young children?
options: Physical complaints, irritability and social withdrawal
slides.why: Young children often show depression through aches, irritability and withdrawal rather than stated sadness.

terms.meaning: Death of a parent, separation, losing a close relationship
Believing nothing one does can change bad outcomes
Pessimistic beliefs about oneself, the world and the future
Major change, rejection or ongoing abuse

slides.heading: After the move
slides.story: When her father loses his job, eight-year-old Chiamaka's family moves from Lagos to a village she does not know. She leaves her best friends, her grades slip, she complains of headaches most mornings and snaps at her siblings. Her new teacher notices she sits alone at break. A school counsellor recognises signs of depression.
slides.takeaway: Major change and loss can trigger childhood depression, which often shows as physical complaints, irritability and withdrawal.

slides.heading: Risk and treatment
slides.body:
Like depressed adults, depressed children are at **high risk of suicide**, so signs must be taken seriously.

Childhood depression is often helped by **cognitive therapy**, **interpersonal** approaches such as **social skills training**, and **family therapy**. **Antidepressant** medication helps some depressed **adolescents**, with careful monitoring.

slides.heading: Bipolar disorder in brief
slides.body:
Depression can take other forms. In **bipolar disorder**, once called **manic-depressive illness**, mood **swings** between **depression** and **mania**.

In children and teenagers, these swings can be harder to recognise and may be mistaken for ordinary moodiness or behaviour problems.

slides.question: Before the 1970s, many clinicians believed that:
options: Depression was common in young children
Pre-adolescent children were unlikely to develop depression
slides.why: Earlier clinicians doubted pre-adolescent depression; research later showed it is real.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'mention five factors that trigger childhood depression': loss, learned helplessness, negative cognitions, low serotonin or norepinephrine, negative life events, major change, rejection or abuse. Also know prevalence (2 to 4%) and child-specific symptoms. Trap: expecting children to report sadness like adults; they often show physical complaints and irritability.
slides.sampleQuestion: Mention five factors that may trigger depression in children.
slides.howToAnswer: List loss, learned helplessness, negative cognitions, low serotonin or norepinephrine activity, and negative life events such as rejection or abuse. Give a one-line example of each.

points: Children can develop depression; 2 to 4% of under-17s have major depression.
Young children show aches, irritability, withdrawal and eating changes.
Triggers: loss, learned helplessness, negative thinking, neurotransmitters, life events.
High suicide risk; treat with cognitive, interpersonal and family therapy.
Bipolar disorder: swings between depression and mania.

questions.stem: About what percentage of children and adolescents under 17 experience major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: Between 2 and 4% of under-17s experience major depression.

questions.stem: Bipolar disorder was formerly called:
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder used to be called manic-depressive illness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common symptom of depression in young children?
questions.explanation: Physical complaints are common in depressed young children.

questions.stem: Learned helplessness as a trigger of depression means:
options: Believing one's actions cannot change bad outcomes
questions.explanation: Repeated uncontrollable bad events teach a sense of helplessness.

questions.stem: Which treatment approach is often helpful for childhood depression?
questions.explanation: Cognitive therapy, interpersonal approaches and family therapy help.

questions.stem: Depressed children, like adults, are at high risk of:
questions.explanation: Suicide risk is high, so signs must be taken seriously.

questions.stem: After being bullied for months, a 10-year-old says 'Whatever I do, they'll still pick on me' and stops trying. This reflects:
questions.explanation: Believing efforts are useless after uncontrollable bad events is learned helplessness.

questions.stem: A teacher notices a pupil has become irritable, eats little, sits alone and complains of headaches daily since his parents' divorce. The most likely concern is:
questions.explanation: These are typical childhood depression signs following a major loss.

questions.stem: A therapist teaches a withdrawn, depressed child how to join games and start conversations. This is:
questions.explanation: Social skills training is an interpersonal approach to childhood depression.

questions.stem: All of the following are triggers of childhood depression EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Low, not high, serotonin activity is linked to depression.

questions.stem: Why was childhood depression underdiagnosed before the 1970s?
options: Clinicians assumed pre-adolescents rarely became depressed
questions.explanation: The belief that young children could not be depressed led to missed cases.

questions.stem: Explanations of childhood depression are described as:
options: Similar to explanations of adult depression
questions.explanation: Loss, helplessness, cognition and neurochemistry explain both.

questions.stem: I. Depression has the highest lifetime prevalence of the emotional disorders. II. Antidepressants help some depressed adolescents. III. Depressed young children usually describe their sadness clearly. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. Young children often show depression through aches and irritability rather than words.

questions.stem: Why might a doctor who sees a child with repeated stomach aches and no physical cause consider depression?
options: Depression in children often appears as physical complaints
It rules out all other conditions
questions.explanation: Unexplained physical complaints can be a sign of childhood depression.

questions.stem: A comprehensive treatment plan for a depressed 12-year-old would most likely include:
options: Cognitive therapy, family involvement and, where appropriate, carefully monitored medication
questions.explanation: Combining cognitive, family and, for some adolescents, medication approaches is most effective.
